name: CAL FIRE Comprehensive
description: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection perimeter data — the primary state fire record covering 1878–2024 with detailed acreage, cause, and perimeter geometry.

metadata.quality: High — official state records with periodic boundary revision

findings: Pre-1993 data may not be as reliable for statistical learning — hand-drawn perimeters and incomplete records. GPS adoption in 1993 dramatically improved data quality, which is why CAL FIRE uses 1993+ data for fire hazard severity zone (FHSZ) mapping. Post-1993: >90% completeness for cause, agency, dates, and size.

~30% of fires have unknown/unidentified causes — fire investigation in post-burn terrain is extremely difficult. Among known causes, lightning accounts for 20% of fires but 39% of burned area (avg 4,800 acres each), while human-caused fires are 80% of ignitions but 61% of acreage (smaller on average). Top human causes: equipment use, debris burning, arson, and campfires.

Seasonality is stark: High Risk Season (Jun-Sep) produces 73% of fires and 84% of burned area. Transition Season (Oct-Jan) is only 12% of fires but 13% of acreage — Santa Ana/Diablo wind events drive disproportionately large fires. Low Risk Season (Feb-May) accounts for just 3% of burned area.

CAL FIRE (State) responds to the most fires (4,194) but USDA Forest Service fires are 2.7× larger on average (5,232 vs 1,921 acres) and account for more total acreage (13.0M vs 8.1M acres). Contract counties handle 1,572 fires; BLM manages 638 fires averaging 1,630 acres each.

Mega-fires (>100K acres) are accelerating: 2 in the 1990s, 9 in the 2000s, 9 in the 2010s, and 18 in the 2020s alone. Mean fire size doubled from 1,766 acres (1990s) to 4,134 acres (2020s). Post-2000 annual burn rate is 3× higher (0.84M vs 0.28M acres/year).

Damage is extremely concentrated — top 1% of fires cause 58% of all burned area, and top 10% cause 93%. The 2020 fire season (4.18M acres) was the worst on record, driven by an unprecedented August lightning siege that ignited fires across all of Northern California simultaneously.

name: MTBS Burn Severity
description: Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity — satellite-derived burn severity mapping for fires ≥1,000 acres (West) and ≥500 acres (East), 1984–2024.

metadata.quality: High — Landsat dNBR validated with field data

findings: 2,051 large fires (>=1,000 acres) in California from 1984-2024, totaling 25.6M acres burned. 77% of records include satellite-derived burn severity data (dNBR thresholds: Low/Moderate/High) — the key differentiator vs CAL FIRE, which has no severity classification.

88% of records are wildfires, 7% prescribed fire, 4% unknown, 1% wildland fire use. Prescribed fires are a small minority, confirming that uncontrolled wildfire overwhelmingly dominates the large-fire landscape in California.

Independently confirms CAL FIRE's acceleration trend via satellite remote sensing — dramatic increases in large fire count, total acreage, and mega-fire (>100K acres) frequency post-2000. The 2020s already show the highest burned area and mega-fire count of any decade despite being incomplete.

High Risk Season (Jun-Sep) fires show different severity profiles than Transition Season (Oct-Jan) fires. Forested areas (Sierra Nevada, Northern CA mountains) tend to show higher severity thresholds, while Southern CA chaparral fires burn intensely but recover faster.

Damage concentration mirrors CAL FIRE — the top 1% of large fires account for a massive share of total burned area. Fire size follows a heavy-tailed log-normal distribution, meaning rare mega-fires determine the character of each fire season.

California consistently ranks among the top US states for both large fire count and total burned area. Western US states collectively show clear post-2000 acceleration, suggesting California's worsening fire regime is part of a broader regional climate-driven trend.

name: FPA Fire Occurrence
description: Fire Program Analysis Fire-Occurrence Database — 2.3 million US wildfire records (1992–2020) with ignition points, cause codes, and discovery/containment dates.

metadata.coverage: All 50 US states — California subset ~300K fires
metadata.quality: Moderate — known reporting gaps for small fires pre-2000

findings: 251,881 California fire records (1992-2020) with 20.9M total acres burned. Unlike CAL FIRE (perimeters) or MTBS (centroids), FPA FOD provides precise ignition point locations — critical for understanding where fires start vs where they spread.

93% of fires are under 10 acres, but just 0.6% of fires (those >=1,000 acres) account for 92% of all burned area. This extreme Pareto concentration means the vast majority of ignitions are quickly contained — the rare ones that escape initial attack determine fire season outcomes.

100% cause attribution using NWCG's standardized 13-category taxonomy — far more consistent than CAL FIRE's numeric codes. Human-caused fires vastly outnumber natural fires in count, but lightning fires burn significantly more acreage per event due to remote ignition locations with delayed detection and response.

FPA FOD uniquely provides discovery time-of-day (82% of records) and containment date (53%). Human fires peak in afternoon hours tied to human activity; natural (lightning) fires show a distinct late-afternoon/evening peak matching thunderstorm timing. Median fire duration is under 1 day — most fires are contained within hours of discovery.

The top general causes are debris burning, equipment use, arson, lightning, and campfires. Debris burning and equipment use dominate human ignitions by count, while lightning dominates by acreage. Cause trends over the 29-year record show relatively stable human ignition rates but increasing variability in lightning-driven years.

1,447 records (0.6%) have direct MTBS linkage, with linked fires averaging 13,039 acres — confirming that FPA FOD's small-fire detail complements MTBS's large-fire severity data. Cross-referencing annual burned area between FPA FOD and MTBS-linked subsets shows strong correlation (r > 0.9), validating consistency across independent federal databases.

name: Topography & Terrain
description: USGS 3DEP elevation data processed into slope, aspect, TPI, TRI, and curvature grids at 800m resolution for all of California.

metadata.records: 6 derived layers: elevation, slope, aspect, TPI, TRI, curvature
metadata.quality: High — lidar-derived source DEM with <1m vertical accuracy

findings: Peak fire occurrence at 400-800m elevation — the chaparral-woodland transition zone.
South- and southwest-facing slopes have 2.3× higher fire density than north-facing slopes.
Terrain ruggedness (TRI) is inversely correlated with fire size — rough terrain limits spread.
Valley bottoms (negative TPI) show higher fire occurrence due to human activity and fuel accumulation.

name: LANDFIRE Canopy Cover
description: LANDFIRE canopy cover percentage at 30m resolution — a key fuel loading proxy showing forest density across California.
findings: Statewide mean canopy cover declined ~8 percentage points from 2001 to 2020, driven by fire and drought mortality.
Dense canopy (>60%) zones show highest fire intensity but lower ignition probability.
Post-2020 recovery signal visible — canopy cover stabilizing after catastrophic 2020 fire season.
Sierra Nevada east-slope canopy loss is the most pronounced regional trend.

name: FVEG Vegetation Classification
description: FRAP Fuel/Vegetation (FVEG) classification data — 68 vegetation types mapped across California, critical for fuel modeling and fire behavior prediction. Includes per-unit vegetation breakdown, fire-vegetation correlation, fuel potential quantification, and post-fire recovery analysis.

metadata.source: CAL FIRE / FRAP FVEG22 + LANDFIRE CC 2024
metadata.coverage: California statewide, all 25 CAL FIRE units
metadata.records: 68 vegetation/fuel classes, 13 WHR13 groups, 8 lifeform categories

findings: Nearly half (49.6%) of California's vegetation is rated High or Moderate fire risk. Brush/shrub is the dominant fuel type at 40.2% of the state, followed by timber (22.0%) and grass (9.0%). Desert Shrub alone covers 22.5% of the state (~87,651 km²) but rarely burns (1.4% burn rate).

Hardwood Forest has the highest burn rate at 57.3% (area burned since 1993), followed by non-desert Shrub at 46.5% and Conifer Forest at 26.3%. Hardwood is 2.6× overrepresented in burned areas relative to its statewide coverage — the most disproportionately fire-affected lifeform.

Shrub has the highest fire density (21.0 fires/1000 km²) followed by herbaceous/grassland (19.7). Fire return intervals are shortest in shrub/chaparral (~8–12 years) and longest in conifer forest (~20–30 years), consistent with fire ecology literature.

Regional vegetation drives fire behavior: Northern CA is 42.5% conifer (forested), Central CA is the most diverse (21.3% shrub, 19.2% agriculture), and Southern CA is 60% shrub/desert-dominated — each region requires distinct fire behavior models.

Fire-prone vegetation fraction per CAL FIRE unit correlates strongly with total area burned — units with >70% fire-prone cover show 2–3× more acreage lost. Composite fuel index identifies continuous high-risk corridors in the Sierra Nevada foothills, Southern California mountains, and North Coast ranges.

Type conversion (conifer → shrubland) is detectable in repeatedly burned areas — early-burn zones (1993–2005) show higher shrub/herbaceous and lower conifer fractions vs. adjacent unburned pixels at matching elevation and aspect.

Post-fire canopy recovery takes 15–25 years to approach unburned baseline (LANDFIRE CC 2024 space-for-time analysis). Reburn areas (2+ fires) show 15–30% lower canopy cover than single-burn pixels. Recovery is faster at lower elevations and in hardwood types, slower at higher elevations in conifers.

WUI exposure hotspots — where high fuel index intersects population density >300/km² — cluster in the Sierra foothills (El Dorado, Nevada counties), San Bernardino mountains, and Santa Barbara/Ventura coast. 800m grid aggregation preserves the dominant vegetation signal with 91% agreement at native 30m resolution.

name: PRISM Climate (CONUS)
description: PRISM climate normals and time series for the contiguous US — temperature, precipitation, VPD, and humidity at 4km resolution from 1895 to present.

metadata.quality: High — station-based interpolation with topographic correction

findings: US mean temperature has risen ~2°F since 1895, with acceleration after 1980.
California ranks in the top 5 states for temperature increase rate.
Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD) — a key fire-weather variable — shows the strongest upward trend of all climate metrics.
Western states show amplified warming compared to the national average.

name: PRISM Climate (California)
description: California-specific PRISM climate analysis — temperature, precipitation, VPD, and humidity at 800m resolution, downscaled from 4km PRISM normals.

metadata.source: Oregon State PRISM Climate Group (CA subset)
metadata.quality: High — dense station network in California

findings: California mean temperature has increased ~4°F since 1895, outpacing national average.
VPD shows the steepest upward trend — critical fire weather metric showing atmosphere's drying power.
Southern California interior valleys show the greatest absolute warming.
Regional analysis identifies 6 distinct climate zones with different fire-climate relationships.

name: PRISM Fire-Climate Overlay
description: Integrated analysis overlaying PRISM climate variables with fire occurrence — quantifying the climate-fire relationship at the 800m grid level.

metadata.quality: Derived — inherits quality from source datasets

findings: VPD explains ~45% of interannual variance in total acres burned — the single strongest climate predictor.
Precipitation deficit in the prior 2 years is a stronger predictor than current-year precipitation alone.
Temperature × wind speed interaction shows a nonlinear threshold above which fire risk escalates rapidly.
Climate-fire coupling is strongest in the Sierra Nevada and weakest in Southern California coastal zones.

name: Census Population & Housing
description: US Census Bureau population and housing data fused with GlobPOP ~1 km gridded estimates, resampled to 800 m resolution (1993–2025) — essential for WUI mapping and fire impact assessment.

metadata.source: US Census Bureau (Decennial + ACS 5-year + PEP) + GlobPOP gridded population
metadata.records: 33 annual COGs (1993–2025), ~652K valid pixels per year
metadata.quality: High — GlobPOP fuses WorldPop + LandScan + GPW + GHS-POP; Census PEP extrapolation 2021–2025

findings: 800 m raster analysis reveals WUI growth frontier: thousands of pixels transitioned from <50 to ≥50 persons/km² since 1993, expanding fire-exposed population.
Composite risk mapping (fire frequency × population density) identifies highest-risk zones in the Sierra foothills, Santa Rosa corridor, and San Bernardino WUI.
Post-fire population change case studies (Camp, Tubbs, Thomas, LNU fires) show 15–40% decline at burn-scar pixels within 5 years.
GlobPOP 800 m data tracks closely with Census PEP at statewide scale (±2%), enabling pixel-level ML features from 1993–2025.

name: Infrastructure Networks
description: Road networks and electrical transmission grid lines — analyzing infrastructure exposure to wildfire risk and ignition proximity.

metadata.source: US Census TIGER/Line + HIFLD Transmission Lines
metadata.quality: Moderate-High — annual TIGER updates, periodic HIFLD refresh

findings: 72% of California wildfires ignite within 1 km of a road — roads are the primary human-access ignition corridor.
Transmission line corridors show 3.4× higher fire density than surrounding areas.
Rural 2-lane roads in chaparral zones have the highest fire-proximity risk score.
Combined infrastructure risk score identifies priority zones for vegetation management.

name: Wind & Fire Weather
description: RAWS station wind data, Energy Release Component (ERC), and Santa Ana wind event analysis — critical fire weather variables for behavior prediction.

metadata.quality: Moderate — station gaps filled with reanalysis

findings: ERC has increased ~40% since 1993 — fuels are drier for longer periods.
Santa Ana wind events correlate with 8 of the 10 most destructive California fires.
Offshore wind events (Diablo winds in NorCal, Santa Ana in SoCal) show increasing overlap with high-ERC periods.
Wind speed alone is a poor fire predictor — the wind × ERC interaction is the key signal.
